Christine Petrosyan 5 min read · Oct 29, 2026 -- Listen Share Set it up to help you, not to do the job instead of you. Press enter or click to view image in full size Where the decision really starts Think about the last thing you bought or switched to. Paying took ten minutes. Deciding took weeks. There was a frustration you kept putting up with, a conversation with someone who had already switched, a price you looked at twice and closed. By the time you opened the product you ended up buying, the decision was made. You were only checking that this one was good enough. The product saw none of that. Its analytics recorded one session, a couple of pages, a purchase or not. Everything that actually led to the decision happened outside the product and before it, where nothing is tracked. The same is true for your users. The problem never starts with your product. Your product comes in late, and the job is to understand what happened before it arrived. Why AI cannot do that part AI knows what you give it. Your documents, your tickets, your dashboards, your transcripts. That is already a lot. But all of it describes what happened inside your product. The weeks before are not in any of those files, so the model has simply never seen them. That would be fine if the model said so. It does not. Ask it why users leave and you get a confident, well-structured answer that reads well in a slide. A few things worth knowing about how it works: It writes a 40%-accurate answer in the same tone as a 95%-accurate one. It agrees with how you asked. “Why is this a good idea?” and “why is this a bad idea?” both get convincing reasons. It fills gaps. Give it eight interviews and ask for ten themes, and you get ten. Two are invented. It cannot tell you what is missing, because it has no way to know. In short, a very fast assistant who never says “I’m not sure.” Work with one long enough and your picture of the market and the users slowly becomes the model’s picture of your own documents. That is how a team ends up well organised and still wrong. Two things to keep doing yourself Both are simple, and both are the first to go when the calendar is full. Use the competitor’s product. AI will build the comparison table in a minute, and it is a good table: features, pricing, what changed last quarter, what the reviews complain about. Read it. Then create an account with your top competitors, pay for the plan a real customer would pay for, and use the product for a week. You will notice things no table has a column for: when they ask for payment, how long it takes before the product feels useful, which step you skipped because it felt like work. Those are usually the real differences. Listen to a user interview yourself. AI will tag themes across thirty calls and find the contradictions. Use that. But listen to at least one full recording, not the summary. Summaries keep what people said and drop how they said it: the pause before “yes, I use it every day,” the laugh when they describe their workaround, the problem they mention twice that never became a theme because it did not fit the question. That is exactly where the weeks before live. A situation most of us have seen: the dashboard shows users dropping at step three of onboarding. The team redesigns step three. The drop barely moves. After a few calls it turns out people were arriving with a different idea of what the product does, picked up from an ad or a friend, and step three was just where that became obvious. No redesign fixes that, and no model would have found it. Three conversations did. How I set it up None of this is an argument against AI. I use it every day: first drafts of PRDs, themes from transcripts, weekly status in three versions for three audiences, explaining our API to me until I understand the constraint. The documentation half of the job always ate the week, and that is exactly the half AI is good at. What it gives back is time, and that time should go to the two things above. What keeps it on the right side of the line is setup, not willpower: Give it context first. One document: what the product is, who uses it, what matters this quarter. Put it in a project so every conversation starts from there instead of from zero. Draft, then attack. Ask for the PRD, then ask what is wrong with the PRD. Keep what survives. Put the routine on a schedule. Competitor changes every Monday, feedback digest every Friday, a decision log after each meeting. Things that should happen without you remembering them. Let it prepare, not attend. It writes the first competitor snapshot; then you open the products. It tags the interviews; then you listen to one. It drafts the questions; then you go and ask them. You can go a lot further than this. Agents that run on their own, connections to your analytics, your ticketing tool, your support inbox, a whole setup that works while you are in meetings. That is a separate article, and a good one. But none of it changes the point. However much of the work you hand over, the reason to hand it over is the same: so you have more time for the product and the users, not less. AI is there to help you, not to be you. What stays with you Being in the product. Being in the user’s week. Noticing what nobody wrote down.
